newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese proud of army's entry into Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Chinese proud of army's entry into Hong Kong.

text.p: Mainland Chinese reacted to the entry on Monday of an advance contingent of Chinese troops into Hong Kong before Beijing's recovery of the British colony with patriotism and pride -- if they knew about it at all.

An advance unit of 40 members of the People's Liberation Army (PLA) drove into Hong Kong on Monday in an historic step toward the reversion of the territory to Beijing's rule after more than 150 years as a colony.
"This is significant because it represents the first action in the return of Hong Kong," said one Beijing office worker. "Before it was all talk.
"Of course, as a Chinese, I am very happy," he said.
But many Chinese were ignorant of the advance unit's arrival -- a source of much controversy in Hong Kong itself -- as mainland media carried no advance coverage of the event.
"I really didn't know about this, and to tell the truth it doesn't really matter that much to me," said one young woman in the Chinese capital.
"But as a Chinese, I think I should probably feel something like 'Ah, Hong Kong has finally begun its return to the motherland'," said the woman, who declined to be identified.

Another woman, visiting the capital from the northern region of Inner Mongolia, also had not heard of the event, a new step in Beijing's highly publicised recovery of the territory. "I'm just a teacher, I don't know anything about politics," she said.
One man reading newspapers in a Beijing park said there had been nothing in the press or on television about the troops, who are to prepare facilities for the future PLA garrison.
"Of course it's a good thing," the man said when asked how he felt about the occasion. "It marks the return (of Hong Kong) after more than 100 years of colonialism."
Chinese officials declined to comment on the significance of the event, and a defence ministry spokesman said he knew nothing about the advance unit's commander, Major-General Zhou Borong.

China's media silence on the event was in contrast to Hong Kong, where the convoy of black Audis and camouflaged army vans received heavy coverage and drew criticism from the territory's Democratic Party.

The unarmed advance PLA soldiers are the first of up to 200 troops that will be phased in before the July 1 handover day as part of the first military presence China has been allowed in the territory in the run-up to the takeover.
Some 10,000 Chinese troops will eventually be stationed in Hong Kong after Britain hands its bustling capitalist outpost back to communist-ruled China.
"These troops are the best of the PLA," the office worker said. "They can speak the language and they know the customs."

The prospect of the PLA's arrival has worried many Hong Kong residents who remember that its tanks charged into Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989 and crushed the student-led democracy movement there, leaving hundreds dead.
"I don't think they will cause any trouble, maybe less than the British troops there," the office worker said.
China has been at pains to soothe fears, parading the elite troops chosen for Hong Kong garrison duty and extolling their virtue, discipline and high education level.
